title: Arise and eat (1 Kings 19:1–8)
hookLine: exhausted Elijah wants to die; an angel brings food and says "Arise and eat"

cards: A message arrives from the palace. Queen Jezebel has heard what happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a promise: by this time tomorrow, you'll be dead.
The man who stood alone against a mountain full of prophets doesn't stand this time. He runs, south, out of the kingdom, to Beer-sheba.

He leaves his servant there and keeps going, alone, a day's journey into the wilderness. He sits down under a broom tree, a scrubby desert bush. And the prophet who faced down a whole mountain says he's done.

teach.b: His words are blunt. It is enough. Now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am not better than my fathers.
Then he lies down and falls asleep. Notice the timing. This isn't Elijah after a failure.

It's Elijah right after Carmel: fire fell from heaven at his word, and now he's under a bush asking to die. The text doesn't scold him for it, or call him weak or faithless. An angel touches him and says: "Arise and eat."

teach.h: A CAKE AND A JAR OF WATER.
teach.b: By his head is a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He eats, he drinks, and he lies back down. No lecture.
Then the angel comes a second time, touches him again, and says it again: arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.
He gets up, eats, drinks, and in the strength of that food, the text says, he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. Look at the order.
Before anyone talks to Elijah about his calling, his fear or his future, someone feeds him and lets him sleep. Twice.
Some readers notice how tender this scene is: the God who sent fire on Carmel sends a meal under a bush.

teach.h: THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.
teach.b: The great conversation is still coming, on the mountain. But first, the body. A tired person can't hear much of anything, so the first word from heaven is the plainest one possible.

how: Jews read Elijah's flight to the wilderness as part of the book of Kings, and it is read in synagogue as a haftarah; the scene is often remembered as a picture of care for someone at the end of their strength.

o: a tall cedar cut to build the Temple
a fruit tree planted at the edge of a field
a desert bush Elijah lay down under, worn out

games.q: arise and eat — tap the pairs.
p: touches him and says arise and eat

s: Elijah fled right after losing on Carmel
he fled right after the fire fell, soon after his victory.
the angel woke him twice to eat
the second time adding: the journey is too great for thee.
the angel rebuked Elijah for despairing
the text has no rebuke here, only food, water and rest.

games.q: you're the angel. the prophet who brought fire down is lying under a bush, asking to die. what do you do first?
o: remind him of his victory on Carmel.
wake him and give him food and water.
games.why: the angel says arise and eat, lets him sleep again, and feeds him a second time. the talk comes later.

practice: Ask your body a plain question, when did I last eat, drink water, or rest, and let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen with a long breath out.
If something heavy is pressing on you, set it beside you for now, the way Elijah's journey waited while he slept.
And if a heaviness like his under the tree is ever yours, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Broom tree. Where an exhausted Elijah collapsed and asked to die, before an angel told him to eat. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: arise, eat, the angel's words in 1 Kings 19:5 and 19:7.

carryVoice: Your line: but first, the body. Bread and rest came before any talk of the road. Day seven hundred sixty-eight, done.
